In some instances of **discipline***,* tangible consequences might need to accompany instructions.
**You are sworn to tell the truth:** See [Lev 5:1](Lev.5.1).
**Fearing people is a dangerous trap:** See [1:7](Prov.1.7); [Luke 12:4-5](Luke.12.4-Luke.12.5).
Agur expresses his ignorance (cp. [Ps 73:22](Ps.73.22), where the psalmist calls himself a *senseless animal*). The first step toward wisdom is acknowledging what we do not know.
This superscription probably refers to the whole of ch [30](Prov.30.1-Prov.30.33).
**Agur son of Jakeh:** Apart from this reference, Agur and Jakeh are unknown. If “from Massa” is the correct reading, then Agur was a non-Israelite (the tribe of Massa is known from Assyrian texts).

In contrast to Agur’s ignorance and powerlessness stands the strength and wisdom of **God** (cp. [Ps 18:30](Ps.18.30)). This is good news to Agur, who understands that God is **a shield to all who come to him for protection**.

Agur requests **two favors** from God: that God will help him not to **lie** (cp. [6:16-19](Prov.6.16-Prov.6.19); [14:5](Prov.14.5), [25](Prov.14.25); [25:18](Prov.25.18); [26:18-19](Prov.26.18-Prov.26.19)) and that he not be given too much or too little. It is not sinful to be rich ([3:9-10](Prov.3.9-Prov.3.10), [15-16](Prov.3.15-Prov.3.16); [10:15](Prov.10.15), [22](Prov.10.22)) or poor ([3:27](Prov.3.27); [11:24](Prov.11.24); [28:27](Prov.28.27); [29:7](Prov.29.7), [14](Prov.29.14)), but Agur wisely wanted to avoid the pitfalls of both.

These verses summarize the character traits that wise people despise. Fools dishonor their parents ([10:1](Prov.10.1); [20:20](Prov.20.20); [Exod 20:12](Exod.20.12); [Deut 5:16](Deut.5.16)), deceive themselves ([Prov 8:7](Prov.8.7)), think they are **pure** when they are **filthy** ([20:9](Prov.20.9)), are proud ([6:17-18](Prov.6.17-Prov.6.18); [11:2](Prov.11.2); [13:10](Prov.13.10); [15:33](Prov.15.33); [16:18](Prov.16.18); [18:12](Prov.18.12); [19:20](Prov.19.20); [29:23](Prov.29.23)), wound others with their words (**teeth like swords***,* see [25:18](Prov.25.18)), and harm the poor ([3:27](Prov.3.27); [11:24](Prov.11.24); [28:27](Prov.28.27); [29:7](Prov.29.7), [14](Prov.29.14)).

The number parallelism (**three . . . no, four**) is a device for presenting a list of poetic examples. This list shows powers that are insatiable and often dangerous. See also [30:18-19](Prov.30.18-Prov.30.19), [21-23](Prov.30.21-Prov.30.23), [29-31](Prov.30.29-Prov.30.31).
The **grave**, which stands for death itself, never seems to have enough—people keep dying ([27:20](Prov.27.20)).

**barren womb:** Women who are unable to have children often long to have them, like Sarah until she gave birth to Isaac, Rebekah until the birth of Esau and Jacob, and Hannah until the birth of Samuel.
The **thirsty desert** and a **fire** consume anything in their path.
People who are callous toward their parents will meet a violent end (see [10:1](Prov.10.1); [19:26](Prov.19.26); [28:24](Prov.28.24); [29:3](Prov.29.3); [30:11](Prov.30.11)).
The writer stands amazed at how one thing moves on another.
The writer expresses horror at sex outside of marriage.
This proverb lists **four** things that **make the earth tremble** because they overturn the order of things.
**who prospers** (literally *who is full of bread*): In the ancient Near East as in much of the non-industrialized world today, having adequate food (bread) was a sign of prosperity.
Another example of number parallelism. Here, small, insignificant animals are surprisingly powerful and resourceful.

**Lemuel,** like Agur, might have been from Massa (see study note on 30:1). Lemuel’s mother’s teaching encourages him to control his lusts (particularly for women and alcohol) so that he might reign justly.
Apart from this passage, Lemuel is unknown.
The admonition not to **waste** energy on lust for **women** echoes earlier warnings (ch [5](Prov.5.1-Prov.5.23); [6:20-35](Prov.6.20-Prov.6.35); [7:1-27](Prov.7.1-Prov.7.27)).
Too much **wine** numbs the senses. A king needs his wits about him and should not overindulge in **alcohol**.
Rather than opening his mouth to drink wine ([31:4-7](Prov.31.4-Prov.31.7)), the king should **speak up** on behalf of the defenseless.
Proverbs ends with a powerful poem celebrating the virtuous wife. The poem’s acrostic arrangement gives an impression of completeness and provides the student with an aid for learning.
No one can **find a virtuous and capable wife** without God’s help ([18:22](Prov.18.22)). Such a woman, like wisdom, is **more precious than rubies** (cp. [3:15](Prov.3.15)).
This wife works to provide food and clothing for her family.
An excellent wife is engaged in commercial enterprises outside her home.

A virtuous wife is generous to the poor, another characteristic of wise people ([11:24-26](Prov.11.24-Prov.11.26); [21:13](Prov.21.13); [22:9](Prov.22.9), [16](Prov.22.16), [22-23](Prov.22.22-Prov.22.23); [28:27](Prov.28.27)).

A capable wife’s industriousness enables her husband to distinguish himself among community leaders. In ancient Israel, **civic leaders** met at the **city gates** to conduct trials and make decisions.
The noble wife’s character exemplifies wisdom. She is coolheaded as she faces future uncertainties. She gives advice in a winsome way.
Those most important to the woman testify to her character, abilities, and achievements.
The book concludes where it began, by affirming the ultimate importance of the fear of **the** **LORD** (see [1:7](Prov.1.7)). A woman’s character is more important than her physical **beauty**.
